Below is a verse-by-verse commentary on Ezekiel 9, drawn from the sources I was able to consult. Where I could not locate material (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan sources specifically), I have noted that limitation.

---

## Ezekiel 9 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Overview

The chapter continues the vision begun in chapter 8. While chapter 8 exposed the idolatrous abominations in the temple, chapter 9 depicts the resulting judgment — the slaughter of the ungodly and the merciful preservation of a faithful remnant. The chapter closes with Ezekiel’s anguished intercession and God’s firm answer.

— Ellicott: [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html)
— Guzik: [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/)

---

### v. 1 — “Then I heard Him call out in a loud voice, saying, ‘Draw near, O executioners of the city, each with a weapon of destruction in hand.’”

**Traditional Reading:** The speaker is the same divine Being as throughout the previous chapter — the Lord God Himself (Ezekiel addresses Him as “Ah, Lord GOD” in v. 8). The “loud voice” expresses the fierceness of divine indignation. The “executioners” (literally “those who bring punishment” or “those who have charge over the city”) are not earthly officers but angelic beings appointed to execute God’s judgment on Jerusalem. The phrase “every man” does not imply humanity; Scripture regularly uses similar language for angels (Gen 18:1–2; Josh 5:13; Dan 8:16). — Ellicott: [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html); Gill: [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm); Bible.org: [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9)

**Grammatical Note:** The Hebrew verb translated “draw near” is actually a Qal perfect (“they have drawn near and abide”), though many translations render it as an imperative. — Bible.org: [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9); NET notes: [classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=9](https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=9)

**Denominational Note — Baptist:** Garner-Howes notes these “executioners” may be understood as “administrative officers in the city,” comparing Isaiah 60:17 and the angelic “watchers” of Daniel 4:13. — [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-9.html)

---

### v. 2 — “And I saw six men coming from the direction of the Upper Gate, which faces north, each with a weapon of slaughter in his hand. With them was another man clothed in linen who had a writing kit at his side. And they came in and stood beside the bronze altar.”

**Traditional Reading:** Six armed men plus the man in linen make seven — the biblical number of completeness. Ellicott notes the man in linen was “among them, but not of them,” distinguishing him from the executioners. His linen garment was the priestly garment (Lev 16:4) and also worn by heavenly beings (Dan 10:5; 12:6), symbolising purity. The “writer’s inkhorn” was a case containing pens, knife, and ink, worn at the girdle by an Oriental scribe. They came from the north — the direction from which the Babylonian invasion would come, and where Ezekiel had just been shown the idolatries (Ezek 8:3, 14). The bronze altar was the altar of sacrifice, the central point of true worship and also the scene of its profanation (Ezek 8:16). — Ellicott: [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html); Guzik: [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/); Gill: [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm); Precept Austin: [preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11)

**Who is the man in linen?** Commentators differ:
- **Ellicott** says he is “simply a necessity of the vision, an angelic messenger” — not Christ, and not the Babylonian god Nebo. — [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html)
- **Gill** identifies him as “the Son of God, in a human form… at the head of them, as their leader and commander… clothed with linen, not in the habit of a warrior, but of a priest; who, as such, had made atonement for the sins of his people.” — [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm)
- **Dr. Constable** notes that “some expositors believed this individual was the Angel of the Lord, the preincarnate Christ… There is no way to prove or disprove this theory. Most interpreters believe he was an angel.” — [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-9.html) (excerpt from search)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** “This one represented no less than an heavenly messenger of the Lord with a special commission… even the son of man… This seventh person, the intercessory high priest, had instead of a slaughter weapon, a writer’s inkhorn.” — [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-9.html)
- **Bible.org:** “He is dressed as a priest… and yet, is angelic and functions as a scribe.” — [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9)

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible):** The six men plus the scribe equal seven, “which was believed by the Babylonians to be the number of planetary deities.” — [classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=9](https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=9)

---

### v. 3 — “Then the glory of the God of Israel rose from above the cherubim, where it had been, and moved to the threshold of the temple. And He called to the man clothed in linen who had the writing kit at his side.”

**Traditional Reading:** The glory of God (the Shekinah) moves from its resting place above the cherubim — either the Ark of the Covenant in the Holy of Holies or the vision-chariot of chapter 1 (cf. Ezek 8:4). This movement to the threshold of the temple signals both that judgment proceeds from the temple itself and that God is beginning to forsake His dwelling. The threshold represents the entrance; God is poised to leave. — Ellicott: [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html); Bible.org: [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9); Precept Austin: [preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11)

**Wiersbe** (Reformed-leaning): “The glory of God moved from the Holy of Holies and began to depart from the temple: ‘Ichabod—the glory has departed’ (1 Sam 4:19–22). Without the glory of God, the temple was just another building.” — [preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11)

**Gill** identifies the speaker as a “divine Person” — the glory of the God of Israel is the same who now gives the command. — [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm)

---

### v. 4 — “‘Go throughout the city of Jerusalem,’ said the LORD, ‘and put a mark on the foreheads of the men sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there.’”

**Traditional Reading — The Mark:** The Hebrew word for “mark” is *taw* (תָּו), the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In the ancient Paleo-Hebrew script, *taw* was written as a cross (X or +). This mark served as a protective sign, like the blood on the doorposts at Passover (Exod 12) and Rahab’s scarlet cord (Josh 2). It identified the righteous for preservation while the ungodly were slain. — Ellicott: [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html); Precept Austin: [preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11); Guzik: [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/)

**Who is marked?** Only those who “sigh and groan” over the abominations — not the “innocent” by worldly standards, but those whose hearts are broken over sin. The remnant is defined by godly grief, not by age, sex, or social standing. This includes men like Jeremiah. — Guzik: [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/); Gill: [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm); Ironside: [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/ezekiel-9.html)

**New Testament parallels:** The mark on the forehead is seen as anticipating Revelation 7:2–3; 9:4; 14:1 (the sealing of the 144,000), and the sealing of believers by the Holy Spirit (2 Cor 1:22; Eph 4:30). — Precept Austin: [preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11); Guzik: [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/)

**The Tau/Cross debate:**

- **Early Church Fathers** (Tertullian, Origen, Cyprian, Jerome) saw the *taw* as a prophetic foreshadowing of the cross of Christ because of its cross-like shape in the old script. — Ellicott: [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html); Precept Austin: [preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11)
- **Feinberg** (Jewish believer): “Christian interpreters have seen a somewhat prophetic allusion to the sign of the cross… Ezekiel, of course, could not have thought of Christian symbolism nor is the passage a direct prediction of Christ’s cross. It is a remarkable coincidence, however.” — [preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11)
- **Gill** (Reformed Baptist, 18th c.) argues *against* the cross-shape theory: “not the Hebrew letter… because in the form of a cross… for this letter has no such form, neither in the characters used by the Jews, nor by the Samaritans, at least in the present character; though Origen and Jerom on the place say that the letter ‘tau’ had the form of a cross in the letters the Samaritans used in their time.” — [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm)
- **Bible.org** warns: “Be careful of allegory. It can make Scripture mean anything!” — [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9)
- **NET notes:** “In ancient Hebrew script this letter was written like the letter X.” — [classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=9](https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=9)

---

### v. 5 — “And as I listened, He said to the others, ‘Follow him through the city and start killing; do not show pity or spare anyone!’”

**Traditional Reading:** Judgment is not delayed; as soon as the righteous are marked, the slaughter begins. This mirrors the deliverance of Lot — judgment waited only until the righteous were secured (Gen 19:22–25). The command to show “no pity” reflects God’s settled determination, not the disposition of the Chaldean instruments (who were already cruel). — Ellicott: [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html); Gill: [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm)

---

### v. 6 — “Slaughter the old men, the young men and maidens, the women and children; but do not go near anyone who has the mark. Now begin at My sanctuary.”

**Traditional Reading:** The list — old, young, maidens, children, women — is deliberately comprehensive and shocking. No category of persons escapes judgment except those with the mark. The command to “begin at My sanctuary” reflects the principle that judgment starts with those closest to God: greater privilege brings greater responsibility. The “elders who were before the temple” are the seventy elders of Ezekiel 8:11, 16, who offered incense to idols. — Guzik: [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/); Gill: [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm); Bible.org: [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9)

**New Testament connection:** This is widely seen as the OT source for 1 Peter 4:17 — “it is time for judgment to begin with the household of God.” — Bible.org: [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9); Precept Austin (Wiersbe): [preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11)

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Sees eschatological significance — “This awaits a final fulfillment, Revelation 7:3–8; 8:5, when the 144,000 redeemed Jews are sealed.” — [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-9.html)

---

### v. 7 — “Then He told them, ‘Defile the temple and fill the courts with the slain. Go forth!’ So they went out and began killing throughout the city.”

**Traditional Reading:** Under the Mosaic law, the touch of a dead body caused ceremonial defilement (Num 19:11). That God commands the temple itself to be defiled with corpses underscores the completeness of judgment. The very sanctuary the people trusted as their protection becomes the epicentre of slaughter. God is about to forsake His sanctuary, so its defilement is part of the judgment itself. — Ellicott: [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html); Gill: [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm)

**Bible.org** notes the three-fold command in this verse: (1) defile the temple, (2) fill the courts, (3) go forth. — [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9)

---

### v. 8 — “While they were killing, I was left alone. And I fell facedown and cried out, ‘Oh, Lord GOD, when You pour out Your wrath on Jerusalem, will You destroy the entire remnant of Israel?’”

**Traditional Reading:** Ezekiel, seeing the slaughter in vision, is overwhelmed. He is “left alone” — in the vision he appears to be the sole survivor in the temple. He falls on his face in intercession, like Moses and Aaron at Korah’s rebellion (Num 16:22). His cry reveals a pastoral heart: he had preached judgment, yet seeing it enacted undoes him. He fears the total destruction of “the remnant” — the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin still in the land. — Guzik: [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/); Ellicott: [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html); Gill: [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm)

**Bible.org** notes the theological tension: “Remember this is a theological vision… This is a prediction of the Babylonian invasions… In the vision there were no survivors. In reality there were. The vision drives home the theological truth with vividness and power! YHWH hates idolatry, especially in His own covenant people!” — [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9)

**Spurgeon** (Reformed Baptist) preached on “I was left”: Spurgeon drew from this verse for a sermon titled “Spared!” delivered in the winter of 1860–1861, emphasising the believer’s preservation in judgment. — [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/ezekiel-9.html)

---

### v. 9 — “He replied, ‘The iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. The land is full of bloodshed, and the city is full of perversity. For they say, “The LORD has forsaken the land; the LORD does not see.”’”

**Traditional Reading:** God answers Ezekiel’s intercession not with mercy but with a justification of the judgment. The iniquity is described with emphatic language: “exceedingly great” (literally “very, very great”). Three charges are laid: the land is “full of blood” (murder, bloodshed), the city is “full of perversity” (perversion of justice, twistedness), and the people have adopted a practical atheism — “the LORD does not see.” This last charge echoes Ezekiel 8:12, where the elders said the same thing in their chambers of idolatry. Denial of God’s providence and omniscience is identified as the root of their lawlessness. — Guzik: [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/); Gill: [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm); Bible.org: [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9)

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** “Denial of the providence and omniscience of God is the source of all lawlessness.” — [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-9.html)

**Spurgeon** also preached on v. 9, contrasting “The iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah is exceeding great” with 1 John 1:7 — “The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” — [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/ezekiel-9.html)

**Textual Note (NET):** The Hebrew word for “perversity” (BDB 642) occurs only here in the OT and may derive from a root meaning “bend” or “twist,” conveying sin as a perversion of God’s standard. — [classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=9](https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=9)

---

### v. 10 — “‘But as for Me, I will not look on them with pity, nor will I spare them. I will bring their deeds down upon their own heads.’”

**Traditional Reading:** God declares He will match their hardness with His own — as they have shown no pity to the poor and needy, He will show them none. The phrase “bring their deeds down upon their own heads” (or “recompense their way upon their head”) is a recurrent formula in Ezekiel (7:3, 4, 8, 9; 11:21; 16:43; 22:31). It expresses the principle of divine retributive justice. There is a grim irony: the idolaters said “the LORD does not see,” and God answers that He will indeed refuse to “see” — that is, refuse to look with pity — when calamity strikes. — Guzik: [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/); Gill: [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm); Bible.org: [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9)

---

### v. 11 — “Then the man clothed in linen with the writing kit at his side reported back, ‘I have done as You commanded.’”

**Traditional Reading:** The chapter closes with the scribe’s simple report. This confirms that the faithful remnant has been marked and preserved before the slaughter began. It is a note of hope amid the horror: even in the severest judgment, God has not forgotten His own. His faithful servants accomplish their tasks.

**Christological reading (Gill):** Gill sees Christ typified here: “Christ, as man and Mediator, sustains the character of a servant; as such he has commands enjoined him, which he has obeyed; he has done all he was to do; he has fulfilled the whole will of God, and wrought out the complete salvation of his people; a report of which he made when here on earth, John 17:4.” — [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm)

**Bible.org** notes the irony: “Angels obey God, but not His creatures made in His image. What irony!” — [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9)

**Ironside** (Brethren): “This was to reassure the prophet concerning those who had humbled themselves before God and mourned because of the sin of Judah.” — [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/ezekiel-9.html)

## Summary of Denominational Distinctives

| Tradition | Key Distinctive on Ezekiel 9 | Source |
|-----------|------------------------------|--------|
| **Baptist** (Garner-Howes) | The man in linen is a heavenly messenger/Christ-figure; the chapter has eschatological fulfilment in Revelation 7 | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-9.html) |
| **Baptist** (Spurgeon) | V. 8 preached as “Spared!”; v. 9 contrasted with cleansing blood of Christ | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/ezekiel-9.html) |
| **Reformed Baptist** (Gill) | Christological: man in linen = Son of God; resists the tau/cross allegory | [mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/9.htm) |
| **Reformed** (Wiersbe) | Emphasis on Ichabod — glory departing; judgment begins with God’s people | [preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_91-11) |
| **Brethren** (Ironside) | The mark as sign of self-judgment; faithful remnant theme | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/ezekiel-9.html) |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Guzik/Enduring Word) | Emphasis on the mark as protective and prophetic, anticipating the cross; practical application for today | [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-9/) |

**Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, Catholic, and Orthodox sources** were not located within the permitted search/fetch limits. The Early Church Fathers’ reading (Tertullian, Origen, Cyprian, Jerome) — seeing the *taw* as prefiguring the cross — is widely cited across traditions (see, e.g., Ellicott and Precept Austin above) and significantly influenced later Catholic sacramental use of the sign of the cross.

## Other Views: Modern Scholarship

- **NET Bible notes:** Notes that the six men plus the scribe = seven, the Babylonian number of planetary deities. The *taw* in ancient Hebrew script was written like an X. The Hebrew word for “perversity” (v. 9) occurs only here in the OT. — [classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=9](https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Eze&chapter=9)
- **Bible.org:** Warns against allegorical readings of the mark; emphasises the vision genre — “in the vision there were no survivors. In reality there were. The vision drives home the theological truth with vividness.” — [new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9](https://new.bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-9)
- **Ellicott:** Rejects both the identification of the man in linen with the Babylonian god Nebo and with Christ. — [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-9.html)
